aliases.name: Hakumen Konmō Kyūbi no Kitsune
aliases.meaning: 'White-Faced Golden-Haired Nine-Tailed Fox' — title used in some otogizōshi

description.summary: A legendary Japanese nine-tailed fox spirit who, disguised as a beautiful court lady, infiltrated the Heian Imperial court and bewitched the Emperor before being exposed and slain on the Nasu plain.
description.full: Tamamo-no-Mae is a legendary figure of late-medieval Japanese narrative, first appearing in Muromachi-period otogizōshi and elaborated through the Edo period. In the canonical legend she is a nine-tailed fox (kyūbi no kitsune) who, having previously corrupted Chinese and Indian rulers in earlier lives (often identified with the Shang concubine Daji and with 'Lady Kayō' of India), arrives in Japan and serves Emperor Konoe (or, in many later sources, Emperor Toba) as the courtesan Tamamo-no-Mae. She is so beautiful and erudite that the Emperor falls under her spell and falls gravely ill. The astrologer Abe no Yasuchika divines her true nature, and the warriors Kazusa-no-suke (Hirotsune) and Miura-no-suke (Yoshiaki) are dispatched to hunt her on the Nasu plain in Shimotsuke (modern Tochigi prefecture), where she is killed. Her vengeful spirit then enters a stone, the Sesshō-seki ('Killing Stone'), which emits poisonous vapours and kills any creature that approaches. The stone is finally exorcised by the Buddhist monk Gennō Shinshō, who shatters it into fragments. The Sesshō-seki at Nasu split visibly in two on March 5, 2022, an event widely reported in Japanese and international press. Some scholarship connects Tamamo-no-Mae to the historical Empress consort Bifukumon-in (Fujiwara no Nariko, 1117–1160).

etymology.origin: Japanese 玉藻 'tamamo' ('jeweled / beautiful seaweed-like duckweed') + 前 'mae' (a respectful title for a lady).
etymology.first_use: Muromachi period (1336–1573), in otogizōshi narrative literature.

related_phenomena.name: Kitsune
related_phenomena.description: Tamamo-no-Mae is the most famous individual kitsune in Japanese folklore

features.description: In her true form she is a nine-tailed fox (kyūbi no kitsune), the highest rank of fox spirit
Described as the most beautiful woman of the court, surpassing all rivals
Some accounts state she glowed with a faint light at night, exposing her supernatural nature

physical.morphology: Shapeshifter alternating between an aristocratic Heian court lady and a gigantic white or golden nine-tailed fox.

abilities.description: Transforms between human and fox form at will
Drains the life force of the Emperor, manifesting as wasting illness
Demonstrates supernatural knowledge of poetry, classics, and esoteric lore in court debate
After death her spirit inhabits a stone that poisons all who approach

patterns: Cycles through royal courts (India → China → Japan) corrupting rulers
Concealment of true form, exposure by court astrologer or priest
Pursuit and slaying by warrior heroes
Posthumous haunting of the place of death

range.description: The legend is centered in Japan, with the climactic events on the Nasu plain in modern Tochigi prefecture. Earlier 'lives' of the fox spirit are set in China (Shang court) and India.

hotspots.name: Sesshō-seki ('Killing Stone'), Nasu Yumoto

location.description: Volcanic rock at Nasu Yumoto Onsen in the Nasu hot-spring area, Tochigi prefecture

hotspots.notes: Site associated with Tamamo-no-Mae's death; the stone visibly split in two on March 5, 2022.

peak_activity_periods.description: Earliest extant otogizōshi versions of the legend
Diffusion in kabuki, jōruri, ukiyo-e, and chapbook literature; 1653 addendum introducing the Sesshō-seki episode

origins.cultural_roots: The legend draws on Chinese fox-spirit traditions (most famously Daji at the Shang court) and on Indian narrative material featuring the 'Lady Kayō' figure, then localizes the cycle within the Japanese Imperial court.
origins.earliest_accounts: Otogizōshi prose narratives of the Muromachi period.
origins.folklore_connections: Closely linked to the Sesshō-seki tradition at Nasu, to Buddhist exorcism narratives around the monk Gennō Shinshō, and to Heian-court historical fiction.

timeline.event: Reign of Emperor Toba ends; the historical period in which the legend later sets the events
The Tamamo-no-Mae legend is in circulation in Muromachi-period otogizōshi prose
timeline.significance: Earliest extant narrative form of the legend

timeline.event: Edo-period addendum introduces the Sesshō-seki ('Killing Stone') episode and the exorcism by the Buddhist monk Gennō Shinshō
timeline.significance: Establishes the canonical post-mortem stone episode

timeline.event: The Sesshō-seki at Nasu Yumoto is found to have split in two
timeline.significance: Widely reported as a 'release' of Tamamo-no-Mae's spirit; geologists attribute the splitting to natural cracking from rainwater penetration
timeline.source: Asahi Shimbun and international press, March 2022

history.modern_era: Tamamo-no-Mae remains a major figure in Japanese popular culture, appearing in Noh and kabuki repertory (e.g. 'Sesshōseki'), in countless anime, manga, and video games (notably the Fate franchise), and in tourism around the Nasu Yumoto onsen area, where the partly broken Sesshō-seki is a registered cultural property of Tochigi prefecture.

notable.name: Splitting of the Sesshō-seki

location.description: Sesshō-seki ('Killing Stone'), Nasu Yumoto Onsen, Nasu town, Tochigi prefecture

notable.description: The Sesshō-seki ('Killing Stone'), the volcanic rock at Nasu Yumoto traditionally identified with the death-place and lingering spirit of Tamamo-no-Mae, was discovered to have visibly split into two pieces on the morning of March 5, 2022. Tochigi prefectural officials attributed the rupture to long-term weathering and water infiltration; commentators noted the cultural resonance with the legend of the fox-spirit's release.

factors: Physical event documented in mainstream press
credibility.notes: A real geological event with a strong folkloric resonance.

physical.name: Sesshō-seki ('Killing Stone')
physical.date: Recorded since the late medieval period; split 2022-03-05
physical.description: Volcanic rock at Nasu Yumoto Onsen, traditionally identified as the petrified remnant of Tamamo-no-Mae's malevolent spirit. Toxic volcanic gases (chiefly hydrogen sulfide) in the surrounding area genuinely kill small animals.
physical.location: Nasu Yumoto Onsen, Tochigi prefecture, Japan
physical.analysis: Real geological feature. Volcanic gas emissions provide a naturalistic explanation for the 'killing stone' tradition.

documentary.name: Tamamo-no-Mae otogizōshi
documentary.description: Earliest extant prose narratives of the Tamamo-no-Mae legend, in the otogizōshi corpus.
documentary.analysis: Primary medieval witness to the legend.

scientific.name: Bifukumon-in identification
scientific.description: Some commentators have proposed that the Tamamo-no-Mae figure is a literary refraction of the historical empress consort Fujiwara no Nariko (Bifukumon-in, 1117–1160), whose political power around Emperor Toba and Emperor Konoe drew controversy.
proponents: Cited in the English-language Wikipedia article on Tamamo-no-Mae
evidence_cited: Chronological proximity of Bifukumon-in's career to the legend's setting

scientific.name: Volcanic gas explanation for Sesshō-seki
scientific.description: The Nasu Yumoto area is volcanically active and genuinely emits hydrogen sulfide and other gases lethal to small animals, providing a naturalistic origin for the 'killing stone' tradition.
evidence_cited: Documented small-animal die-offs in the Nasu hot-spring zone

folklore.beliefs: Tamamo-no-Mae is a paradigmatic example of the dangers of foreign or supernatural influence at court and of the protective role of Buddhist clergy and court diviners. She also exemplifies the cross-cultural figure of the seductive fox spirit shared with China and Korea.

indigenous.significance: Part of the living Japanese cultural and religious imagination, with active veneration and tourism at Nasu Yumoto.
indigenous.sensitivity_note: Treat the Sesshō-seki and Nasu shrines as living cultural sites rather than mere folkloric curiosities.
indigenous.respect_guidelines: Refer to academic Japanese-studies sources alongside English Wikipedia; cite the Sesshō-seki as a registered cultural property of Tochigi.

film_tv: Tamamo-no-Mae appears in numerous Japanese television dramas and animated series, often as a femme-fatale archetype
